title: Ratio and Direct Proportion
kicker: Checkpoint 6 Maths · Number · Ratio and proportion
summary: Understand ratio and direct proportion: write and simplify equivalent ratios, scale recipes and prices with the unitary method, and share amounts using bar models.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand what it means when two quantities are in direct proportion — when one is multiplied by a number, the other is multiplied by the same number (6Nf.12)
Use what you know about equivalence to find, simplify and use equivalent ratios, e.g. 2 : 3 = 6 : 9 (6Nf.13)

blocks.text: Ratio and proportion are about **comparing amounts** and **scaling them up or down fairly**. You use them when you make a recipe for more people, mix paint or juice, read a map or share sweets. The big idea is the same as for equivalent fractions: multiply or divide **both** parts by the **same** number.
Key words

items: ratio
نسبة — compares one part with another part, written with a colon, e.g. 2 : 3 ('for every 2 … there are 3 …')
proportion
تناسب / جزء من الكل — compares a part with the whole, e.g. '2 in every 5' = 2/5
equivalent ratios
نسب متكافئة — ratios that compare the same way, e.g. 2 : 3 = 4 : 6 = 6 : 9
simplest form
أبسط صورة — the ratio cannot be divided any more, e.g. 12 : 18 → 2 : 3
direct proportion
تناسب طردي — two amounts that increase or decrease by the same multiplier
unitary method
طريقة الوحدة — find the value for ONE first, then multiply
scale up / scale down
تكبير / تصغير — multiply / divide all amounts by the same number
share in a ratio
تقسيم بنسبة — split a total into parts that follow a ratio

blocks.text: 1. What is a ratio?

A ratio compares **part with part**. In the pattern below, for every 2 yellow tiles there are 3 blue tiles. We write yellow : blue = 2 : 3 and say 'two to three'. **The order matters**: blue : yellow is 3 : 2.

blocks.text: **Proportion** compares a **part with the whole**. In each group there are 5 tiles and 2 are yellow, so the proportion of yellow tiles is '2 in every 5', which is the fraction 2/5. Blue tiles are 3 in every 5 = 3/5. To change a ratio into a proportion, add the parts to find the whole: 2 + 3 = 5.

rows: For every 2 yellow there are 3 blue
For every 1 teacher there are 8 pupils

blocks.text: 2. Equivalent ratios and simplest form
Equivalent ratios work exactly like equivalent fractions. **Multiply or divide both parts by the same number** — never add or subtract.

To write a ratio in its **simplest form**, divide both parts by their **highest common factor** (HCF). If you do not spot the HCF, divide by any common factor and repeat until there are no more common factors.

items: To find a missing number, find the multiplier first: 3 : 5 = ☐ : 35. 5 × 7 = 35, so ☐ = 3 × 7 = 21.
Check: divide the new ratio by the same number — 21 : 35 ÷ 7 = 3 : 5 ✓

blocks.text: 4. Direct proportion

Two quantities are in **direct proportion** when they grow or shrink **together by the same multiplier**: if you buy 2 times as many pens, you pay 2 times as much; one third of the pens cost one third of the money. Zero pens cost $0. The ratio between the two quantities always stays the same.

blocks.text: The safest method is the **unitary method**: find the value for **one**, then multiply. When the numbers are friendly you can also scale in one step (e.g. 4 people → 12 people is × 3).

In this table every amount of flour is the number of cakes **× 200**. That is what direct proportion looks like in a table: the same multiplier links every pair. If you plot the pairs on a graph, the points lie on a **straight line through 0**.

blocks.text: 5. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Write 12 : 18 in its simplest form. [1]
Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. HCF = 6. 12 ÷ 6 = 2, 18 ÷ 6 = 3. **Answer: 2 : 3.** Common mistake: dividing only once by 2 and stopping at 6 : 9.
**Worked example 2** — Write the missing number: 3 : 5 = ☐ : 35 [1]
5 → 35 is × 7. So 3 × 7 = **21**. Common mistake: 3 + 30 = 33 (adding the same amount instead of multiplying).
**Worked example 3** — For every 2 yellow tiles there are 3 blue tiles. (a) There are 12 yellow tiles. How many blue tiles are there? (b) What fraction of all the tiles are yellow? [2]

items: (b) Each group has 2 + 3 = 5 tiles, and 2 are yellow: **2/5**. (Check: 12 out of 30 = 2/5 ✓.) Common mistake: answering 2/3, which compares yellow with blue, not with all the tiles.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A recipe uses 300 g of rice for 4 people. How much rice is needed for 10 people? [2]

Unitary method: 1 person needs 300 ÷ 4 = 75 g. 10 people need 75 × 10 = **750 g**. Another way: 2 people need 150 g, and 10 = 5 × 2, so 150 × 5 = 750 g. Mark scheme style: M1 for 75 (or 150 for 2 people) seen, A1 for 750.
**Worked example 5** — Tick the table that shows direct proportion. Explain your choice. [1]

rows: Table A: litres of juice → cost

blocks.text: **Table A ✓.** Every cost is the number of litres × 3. In Table B, 4 tickets should cost 4 × $5 = $20 if it were direct proportion, but they cost $18.
**Worked example 6** — Sami and Nada share 35 sweets in the ratio 3 : 4. How many sweets does each get? [2]
3 + 4 = 7 parts. 35 ÷ 7 = 5 sweets per part. Sami: 3 × 5 = **15**. Nada: 4 × 5 = **20**. Check: 15 + 20 = 35 ✓ (see the bar model above). Common mistake: dividing 35 by 3 and by 4.
**Worked example 7** — 3 pens cost $4.50. How much do 7 pens cost? [2]
1 pen: 4.50 ÷ 3 = $1.50. 7 pens: 1.50 × 7 = **$10.50** (see the double number line). Estimate: 7 is a bit more than twice 3, so a bit more than $9 ✓.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding instead of multiplying: 2 : 5 → 8 : 11 ✗. Correct: 2 : 5 = 8 : 20.
Writing the ratio in the wrong order. 'Boys to girls' means boys first.
Mixing up ratio and fraction: in 3 : 7, the fraction of the first part is 3/10, not 3/7.
Sharing in a ratio by dividing the total by each number of the ratio instead of by the total number of parts.
Not simplifying fully: 6 : 9 still has a common factor 3 → 2 : 3.
Assuming every relationship is direct proportion — check that the same multiplier works for every pair (and that 0 matches 0).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Patterns of tiles, beads or counters: 'For every 2 red there are 3 blue …' — find the missing number or write the ratio.
Missing-number equivalent ratios, e.g. 4 : ☐ = 12 : 27, and 'Write in its simplest form'.
Recipes and prices ('6 pancakes need 150 ml of milk …') — write the value for one, or a friendly step, in your working for the method mark.
Complete a table of values that are in direct proportion, or choose which table/graph shows direct proportion.
'Is … correct? Explain' — say yes or no and give the mathematical reason (multiply both parts by the same number).
Ratio and proportion can appear on either paper; with a calculator on Paper 2 the numbers may be less friendly, but the method is the same.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Ratio and direct proportion — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. Write ratios like 2:3. Type only the number for money and measurements.

questions.q: Write the ratio 15 : 25 in its simplest form.

questions.e: 4 × 5 = 20, so multiply the other part by 5 as well: 7 × 5 = **35**.
6 : 8 simplifies to 3 : 4. 9 : 12 ÷ 3 = 3 : 4 ✓. 12 : 14 = 6 : 7 (adding 6 to both is not allowed), 3 : 5 is different, and 8 : 6 is in the wrong order.

questions.q: In a wall pattern, for every 3 red tiles there are 2 white tiles. There are 15 red tiles. How many white tiles are there?
questions.e: 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so the pattern repeats 5 times. 2 × 5 = **10 white tiles**. (3 : 2 = 15 : 10.)

questions.q: In a class, 3 in every 5 pupils are girls. There are 30 pupils in the class. How many are girls?
questions.e: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 groups of 5 pupils. Each group has 3 girls: 3 × 6 = **18 girls**. (3/5 of 30 = 18.)

questions.q: Which table shows two quantities in direct proportion?
c: Age 2, 4, 6 years → Height 80 cm, 100 cm, 115 cm
questions.e: In direct proportion you always multiply by the same number. Pay = hours × 6 every time (6, 12, 24) ✓. Pens: 3 × 2 = 6, not 5. Height does not double when age doubles. Boxes: 3 × 10 = 30, not 20.

questions.q: 5 notebooks cost $8.50. What do 3 of the same notebooks cost?
A recipe for 6 pancakes uses 150 ml of milk. How much milk is needed for 15 pancakes?
questions.e: 150 ÷ 6 = 25 ml for 1 pancake. 25 × 15 = **375 ml**. (Or: 3 pancakes need 75 ml, and 15 = 5 × 3, so 75 × 5 = 375.)

questions.q: Write the ratio of yellow tiles to blue tiles in its simplest form.
questions.e: Count: yellow = 2 + 2 = 4, blue = 3 + 3 = 6. Yellow : blue = 4 : 6 = **2 : 3** (÷ 2). Yellow is written first because the question says 'yellow to blue'.

questions.q: Ali and Rana share $40 in the ratio 3 : 5. How much does Rana get?
Hana mixes 2 cups of orange juice with 5 cups of water. She wants the same taste using 8 cups of orange juice. How many cups of water does she need?
questions.e: 2 × 4 = 8, so multiply the water by 4 too: 5 × 4 = **20 cups**. (11 comes from wrongly adding 6 to both parts.)

questions.q: Omar says, '2 : 3 and 3 : 4 are equivalent ratios, because I added 1 to both numbers.' Is Omar correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: No / Omar is not correct. 1 mark: a correct reason, e.g. equivalent ratios are made by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number, not adding; or a counter-example such as 2 : 3 = 8 : 12 but 3 : 4 = 9 : 12; or 2 out of 5 is not the same proportion as 3 out of 7. Do not award the first mark without a reason.
questions.e: **No.** To make an equivalent ratio you multiply or divide both parts by the same number. Check with a common part: 2 : 3 = 8 : 12 and 3 : 4 = 9 : 12 — the first parts are different, so the ratios are not equivalent.

questions.q: A car uses 6 litres of fuel to travel 75 km. At the same rate, how far can it travel on 10 litres?
questions.e: 1 litre: 75 ÷ 6 = 12.5 km. 10 litres: 12.5 × 10 = **125 km**. (Or 2 litres → 25 km, and 10 litres = 5 × 2 litres → 5 × 25 = 125 km.)

questions.q: In a bag the ratio of red counters to blue counters is 3 : 7. What fraction of the counters are red?
questions.e: 3 + 7 = 10 parts in total, and 3 of them are red. Red = **3/10** of the counters. (3/7 compares red with blue, not red with all the counters.)

blocks.title: Remember
items: A ratio compares part with part (2 : 3); a proportion compares part with the whole (2 in every 5 = 2/5).
Equivalent ratios: multiply or divide BOTH parts by the same number — never add.
Simplest form: divide both parts by the HCF (12 : 18 = 2 : 3).
Sharing a total in a ratio: add the parts, find one part, then multiply.
Direct proportion: the same multiplier links every pair; use the unitary method (find one first).
